evidence: src/application/dtos.ts: `toUserDto`, `toProjectDto` and `toTaskDto` are the only mappers, and every use case returns through them.

src/application/add-task-use-case.ts and src/application/list-project-tasks-use-case.ts each repeat the `projects.findById` existence check that throws `NotFoundError`; this is simple orchestration, not a domain rule.
src/application/assign-task-use-case.ts and src/application/mark-task-done-use-case.ts delegate state changes to `task.assignTo` and `task.markDone`, so the rules stay in the domain.

src/application/create-project-use-case.ts and src/application/create-user-use-case.ts use `ids.next()` with the domain factories `Project.create` and `User.create`, the same pattern as AddTaskUseCase.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: All seven files serve one concern: application use cases for the project/task/user domain, plus the DTOs they share. Each use case has a single `execute` method. Each takes domain repository and IdGenerator abstractions through its constructor. Each returns DTOs through the mappers in dtos.ts (`toTaskDto`, `toProjectDto`, `toUserDto`), so the mapping rule lives in one place. Domain rules stay in the domain (`Task.create`, `task.assignTo`, `task.markDone`, `Project.create`, `User.create`). The use cases don't bypass these abstractions or duplicate domain invariants. Two things are minor. The "project not found" check appears in both AddTaskUseCase and ListProjectTasksUseCase, but it is a one-line existence check that raises `NotFoundError`, not a business invariant worth centralizing. MarkTaskDoneUseCase takes a bare `taskId` string where the others take an input DTO, which is a small style inconsistency and not a boundary violation.
